title: Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it and how to view it safely

paragraphs.en: On Wednesday evening, millions of Europeans will experience a celestial treat: a solar eclipse. A wide band of north and central Spain, plus a sliver of Portugal and parts of Greenland and Iceland will experience a rare total eclipse. The light of the setting sun will be virtually blocked out across much of western Europe, including the UK, France, Belgium, Switzerland and northern Italy.
A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between the Earth and the sun, resulting in the moon casting a shadow on the Earth.

Viewers see a total solar eclipse when the sun’s light is fully blocked by the moon – meaning they are in the umbra of the moon’s shadow – and a partial solar eclipse when only part of the light is blocked, meaning they are in the penumbra of the moon’s shadow.

“The moon and sun have to line up precisely for the moon to fully cover the sun and for you to see a total eclipse,” said Dr Megan Argo, a reader in astrophysics at the University of Lancashire and the vice-president of the Society for Popular Astronomy. “Because the orbit of the moon is slightly tilted, it doesn’t appear to cross the disc of the sun from our perspective each time it orbits the Earth.”

Whether viewers see a total or partial eclipse – or no eclipse at all – depends upon their location on the Earth’s surface. “You have to be right in the middle of the shadow to see a total eclipse, and that is quite a narrow track on the Earth’s surface,” said Argo.

This total eclipse will be the first in mainland Europe in two decades. The last event of this kind visible from the UK occurred in 1999, when parts of Devon and Cornwall were in the path of totality. The next total solar eclipse visible in the UK is not due to occur until 2090.

While the country will only experience a partial solar eclipse on Wednesday, experts are enthusiastic, noting the next comparable event visible in the UK will be in 2081. “This is the best [solar] eclipse that we’ve had in the UK since 1999. There have been a few other partial eclipses, but not one that’s this deep, which has this percentage of the sun eclipsed by the moon,” said Argo.
